answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: We find the proposed equation appropriate. The approach, which multiplies electricity consumption (MWh) by the marginal emission rate (MER) for each hour and aggregates the results, is appropriate because it accurately reflects the fact that power systems exhibit different emission characteristics across hours. Since it is well established that the emission impacts of electricity vary substantially depending on when electricity is consumed or procured rather than on annual averages, the AMI proposal to evaluate emission changes using hourly data is consistent with the principles of consequential assessment.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: Electricity‑related project emission impacts should be calculated and reported on an annual basis. Because marginal emission rates (MERs) and underlying power‑system conditions change from year to year, evaluating emission impacts only once over the project’s lifetime would produce results that diverge significantly from actual conditions. The AMI proposal also outlines a framework in which emission impacts are assessed for each reporting year, and this approach allows system changes to be captured more accurately.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Ensuring that additionality assessments can be applied fairly across diverse markets and policy environments, while accurately capturing the material contribution that corporate actions make to the power system, is essential. From this perspective, it is most appropriate for the framework to require both the Regulatory Test and the Contract/Tenor Test as its core elements.
The Regulatory Test provides the fundamental screen to exclude actions that are mandated by law or policy, ensuring that only voluntary corporate actions are assessed; this is aligned with the existing GHG Protocol. The Contract/Tenure Test captures the extent to which long‑term contractual commitments supported the project’s investment decision, and the AMI proposal similarly treats this as a key indicator of additionality. Taken together, these two tests allow for a fair assessment of whether a company’s commitment had a substantive influence on the project, while filtering out mandatory deployment and minimizing cross‑regional inconsistencies.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
When considering the practical feasibility of additionality tests, it is essential that end‑users be able to make determinations based on information they can reasonably obtain and verify themselves. From this standpoint, the Regulatory Test and the Contract/Tenor Test are appropriate required criteria, as the information required for both tests is clear and can be reliably confirmed by end‑users.

The Regulatory Test merely requires checking publicly available information to determine whether an action is mandated by law or policy, and its evaluation criteria are relatively stable, enabling end‑users to assess it without ambiguity. Similarly, the Contract/Tenor Test can be evaluated directly using information contained in the company’s own contractual documents—such as contract duration, start date, and execution terms—making it possible to apply objective and verifiable judgment.

By contrast, the Financial Analysis Test often depends on confidential project‑developer information such as IRR assumptions or cost structures, making it difficult for end‑users to accurately assess on their own. The Timing Test is not suitable as a uniform criterion, as the timing of PPA execution varies significantly across regions. In markets like Japan, where approvals take significant time, basing eligibility solely on pre‑construction contracts would not reflect actual conditions. The Barrier Test faces similar limitations: institutional, technical, and market barriers vary significantly across regions, and the evidence required to demonstrate such barriers frequently relies on internal developer information that end‑users cannot independently verify. The Common Practice Test also poses challenges because definitions of “comparable projects” differ widely across markets, and available market data are not uniform, creating substantial inconsistency in how judgments would be made.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text:
While designing additionality tests that account for regional differences may be theoretically reasonable, introducing region‑specific combinations of tests from the outset would increase complexity and impose greater practical and explanatory burdens on reporting entities. This, in turn, could hinder the broader adoption of reporting and disclosure. Because the AMI framework is intended to quantify and report the emission impacts of corporate actions, it is important to prioritize a set of common rules that can be applied consistently across countries and regions, thereby ensuring comparability and operational feasibility.
Regional differentiation may be considered in the future. However, at the initial stage, it is more practical to establish broader, more universally applicable criteria and begin implementation under conditions that are straightforward to apply.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
The level of rigor required for additionality tests should be calibrated to the type of claim an organization seeks to communicate. For association‑based claims, where the objective is simply to demonstrate a connection between the corporate action and renewable energy, it is sufficient for basic conditions—such as the Regulatory Test and the Contract/Tenor Test—to be met.
In contrast, when an organization wishes to assert that its actions influenced the realization of the project itself—a causality-based claim—stronger evidence is necessary. In such cases, it is appropriate to incorporate supplemental tests that support causal attribution, such as the Financial Analysis Test, the Barrier Test, and the Timing Test.
By scaling the strictness of the required evidence in proportion to the strength of the claim, it becomes possible to conduct evaluations that are both flexible and suited to practical circumstances. This graduated approach also facilitates practical implementation of the framework and supports a more workable reporting system.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: We recommend grid regions as the appropriate spatial granularity. Grid regions capture geographic differences in marginal emission rates and therefore provide higher accuracy than national or broad average emission factors, while avoiding excessive complexity. Since they can leverage existing market data, grid‑region boundaries are easier to standardize and help ensure the reliability of consequential accounting results.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: We recommend annual reporting. Assessing emission impacts each year by multiplying procured electricity volumes with hourly and regional marginal emission rates enables more effective progress tracking and continuous improvement. Because grid emission factors and supply–demand conditions fluctuate from year to year, a one‑time, aggregate assessment cannot accurately capture actual emission impacts. Annual reporting also aligns with the settlement and reporting cycles of VPPAs and long‑term PPAs, which are typically accounted for on a yearly basis. Moreover, disclosing data annually enhances transparency and comparability, thereby supporting companies in meeting their additionality objectives.
